Rules / Correctness

SK2009 An enum switch statement omits declared members

A switch statement over a non-flags enum covers most of it, omits the rest, and has no catch-all.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

A switch statement that silently falls through when a new enum member is added turns a closed decision into an accidental default, and unlike a switch expression the compiler says nothing about it. Listing every value makes the decision explicit and makes future additions show up at the switch that needs a policy.

Example

Instead of:

switch (color) {
    case Color.Red: return 1;
    case Color.Green: return 2;
}

return 0;

Write:

switch (color) {
    case Color.Red: return 1;
    case Color.Green: return 2;
    case Color.Blue: return 3;
}

return 0;

When it does not fire

⚠ The switch *expression* is the compiler's and this rule does not look at one. CS8509 names the uncovered value and CS8524 the undeclared one, both on by default, so ADR-008 leaves the form alone — probed rather than recalled: the expression draws CS8509, the identical switch written as a statement draws nothing at all. ⚠ A statement covering a minority of the enum is a filter, not a forgotten case (#280): falling out of a switch statement continues at the next statement, which is the design of switch (modifier.Kind()) { case SyntaxKind.AsyncKeyword: return false; }. The rule reports only where the omitted values are no more numerous than the handled ones, which on Skala's own tree took the rule from 14 findings to 1 and removed every false positive. ⚠ The recall this costs is real: a ten-member enum with three handled and seven genuinely forgotten is now silent. The rule also excludes [Flags] enums, whose combinations are intentionally open, and any switch with default, discard, var or declaration catch-all handling. It skips pattern forms other than constants and or combinations rather than guessing which values a relational, negated or recursive pattern covers. Enum aliases are compared by constant value, so handling one alias handles all aliases with that value, and aliases count once on both sides of the comparison. No fix is offered because the correct behavior for a missing value is a domain decision.

Configuration
